newsitem.title: GERMANY: IG Metall expects to start national wage talks.
newsitem.headline: IG Metall expects to start national wage talks.

text.p: The German IG Metall engineering trade union was on Friday locked in internal debate on whether to confirm it was ready to talk with employers on sick pay and further 1997 wage demands.
The meeting started at 0830 GMT and a spokesman said he did not expect the board meeting to finish before 1200 GMT. A news conference is scheduled to take place after the meeting ends.

Earlier a spokesman said the union was expecting to hold a summit meeting with employers association Gesamtmetall on Monday and that talks would include the sick pay issue in overall 1997 wage negotiations.
The spokesman said however he was "quite pessimistic about the chances for an overall wage agreement."
"The positions are currently so wide apart," he said.
Gesamtmetall responded in a statement that employers would enter into talks on Monday with the aim of reaching a wage deal that did not place an additional burden on companies.
"We must not produce cost increases if we want to stop the dramatic job losses," the association said in a statement.

The association said the metalworking and electrical engineering sectors had lost about 142,000 jobs between August 1995 and August 1996, according to data released by the Federal Statistics Office on Friday.
"That means the pace of job losses has doubled since the beginning of 1996," Gesamtmetall said.
The dispute over cuts in sick pay is threatening to throw German industrial relations into turmoil ahead of wider 1997 wage talks.

At issue is a federal law passed in September aimed at allowing employers to cut sick pay allowances from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, a move which would shave some 12 billion marks off German industry's labour costs.
Germany has some of the most generous sick pay and holiday provisions in the world.

Industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG, the first large company seeking to implement the law, was earlier this month forced to delay the cuts after more 100,000 of its workers walked out, protesting that it breached existing wage contracts.

Werner Stumpfe, chairman of the Gesamtmetall employers group, has stated as an "absolute pre-condition" for future negotiations that the issue of sick pay and other benefits be included in wider 1997 wage talks.
IG Metall for its part is demanding that Gesamtmetall make clear its final position on sick pay by October 23 -- a day before a second day of countrywide protests in the sector has been planned.

German business, clammering for reductions in labour costs, will be trying to secure a deal that includes not only sick pay cuts but also reductions on existing benefits such as holiday pay and generous Christmas bonuses.

Unless real reductions in overall employment costs are available, Gesamtmetall has said it could not agree even to the 1997 real wage freeze IG Metall has said it would settle for in exchange for job protection guarantees.
